Question: As a teacher, what is the harshest truth a student has ever taught you?
Old_Answer: I was teaching a freshman Calculus course for Biology Sciences, and accidentally overheard a heated discussion between some students in between classes. One of them was a Muslim student called Anand, and he ferociously objected to the theory of evolution (which was obviously very important in the Biology curriculum). One of the professors had explained the evolution of movement in seahorses — a complex and rather mysterious research domain which utilizes theoretical mechanics and differential geometry — and as soon as the word “evolution” had been mentioned, Anand rejected every word of it. Upon being asked by another student whether those really were Anand’s honest thoughts — even though he had seen abundant proof of the contrary — Anand clearly hesitated and said: “I am simply not allowed to think otherwise.” It revealed the shocking truth that this young man was fighting against choices he did not want to make, but somehow he had started to understand that what was (really) going on in Nature, was vastly different than what had been taught to him since childhood. Still, his hesitance showed that a seed had certainly been planted in the mind of this young man. And maybe, just maybe this one would germinate. SOURCES: GIF taken from GIPHY.
Answer_with_writing_sample: As a teacher, I often found myself ready to impart wisdom to my students, only to be blindsided by a lesson that came straight from the mouth of a child. There was this one instance that still makes me pause — a bright-eyed, seemingly carefree young girl who, during a particularly chaotic discussion on life’s challenges, simply asked, “Why do you always say you’re busy when you could just spend time with us?” The bluntness of her question hit harder than I expected. Here I was thinking I was teaching them about responsibility and time management, while she was teaching me about presence, connection, and the importance of valuing what truly matters. It was a brutal wake-up call that made me realize the gap between intention and reality. In a way, her honesty stripped the layers of educator pride away and reminded me of the simple truth that sometimes, it’s not about how much we know, but how much we care. And boy, did I need that reminder. SOURCES: Life lessons from the classroom.
Answer_with_user_profile: As a teacher, one of the harshest truths I have learned from my students is the realization of my own limitations in understanding their diverse backgrounds and individual struggles. Often, we enter the classroom with preconceived notions about learning and behavior, thinking we can easily reach every student. However, I have encountered students with deeply personal challenges—some dealing with family issues, mental health struggles, or socio-economic hardships—that shape their educational experience in ways I could never fully comprehend. One particular student, who frequently disrupted class, taught me this lesson most profoundly. After a candid conversation, I discovered he was grappling with the recent loss of a parent and was struggling to find stability in his life. This moment was a wake-up call for me; it highlighted that my role as an educator extends far beyond delivering lessons and grading assignments. It’s about fostering an environment of empathy, understanding, and support. I realized that my effectiveness as a teacher hinged not only on my knowledge of the subject matter but also on my ability to connect with my students on a human level—acknowledging their stories, respecting their journeys, and creating a classroom atmosphere where they felt seen and valued. This truth has profoundly reshaped my approach to education, reminding me to embrace humility and compassion in my teaching practice and recognizing that sometimes, the most valuable lessons come not from the curriculum but from the very students I seek to teach.
Answer_with_full_information: As a teacher, I once encountered a student who taught me one of the harshest truths about education and personal growth: the realization that not all students are equally ready to learn, and this reality is often influenced by circumstances beyond their control. During a particularly challenging academic year, I had a bright student who initially showed great promise. However, as the months progressed, it became glaringly apparent that intense family pressures—and the emotional toll they wrought—were overshadowing his academic performance. No amount of enthusiasm or engaging lessons could penetrate the walls of his distress. It was during this tumultuous period that I had an epiphany: education is not just about imparting knowledge; it’s about meeting students where they are and recognizing their unique challenges. This student’s struggle illuminated the fact that an effective educator must cultivate empathy and understand that a one-size-fits-all approach simply doesn’t work. There’s a profound need to harness compassion, creating an environment where students feel safe to express their difficulties and seek help. This lesson reshaped my teaching philosophy, pushing me to advocate for a more holistic approach to education—one that acknowledges the emotional and social dimensions of learning. It was a tough pill to swallow, realizing that enthusiasm could not substitute for understanding, but it ultimately made me a more effective and empathetic educator, dedicated to fostering genuine relationships with my students. After all, the true heart of teaching lies in unlocking not just the mind, but also the spirit of each individual.

Question: A person has told me that chemotherapy and radiotherapy are toxic and deadly, that they can give me a cure for my cancer through natural medicine. Is he right?
Old_Answer: The herbal treatment. I know of at least two people who tried it (instead of classical cancer therapies), and they are the exact two people who vanished in the most painful way. One was a patient of my girlfriend. A young man with a peeing problem that turned out to be a prostate thing. He wanted to have many more girlfriends libido-wise, he wanted to perform, he did NOT want to wear diapers, he wanted to be erected, he wanted to be a man (in his own language). And he declined. He declined every single therapy (prostatectomy, psychiatric evaluation and help, hormone treatment) because his brother would prepare herbal emulsions and the like to cure him. And surprise, surprise — he turned into pieces under the supervision of his loving brother who did not know squat. The second subject is an actress called Sylvia Millecam.[1] A Dutch icon know for her uncanny talent to improvise, fast intuition and beauty. But Sylvia also had an uncanny obsession for (her own) beauty, and she would do anything to keep it that way. A mastectomy ? — no thanks (‘they” define me as an actress). Chemotherapy ? — how will I look afterwards ? So Sylvia, as an avid supporter of alternative medicine, chose to follow a guru who claimed to cure cancer and every single other disease known to mankind through her own radiating radiation into water (usually recorded months in advance) and through radio talk (also usually recorded months in advance), and her guru urged her to stop having classical medical treatments, and drink her radiated water, and listen to her radiated words instead. At a not-so-small cost, as you might have expected. And Sylvia died before she reached the age of 45 — the tumor had ruined her body as if a bomb had exploded.[2] She was a mere skeleton. She was a mere copy of a thought. She was someone who could have been saved, but who believed the herbal woman with that very big fee. These are some of the few people I have known who tried the natural course. And who were obliterated on the way. SOURCES: Dissection of the female abdomen, showing the kidneys, gravid (?) uterus, ovaries and fallopian tubes, with the arteries and blood vessels indicated in red. Colored lithograph by J. Roux, 1822. Wellcome Collection.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The short, straightforward answer is NO. That person is either deeply misinformed or, frankly, trying to sell you something. Sure, the word "toxic" gets thrown around a lot regarding chemotherapy and radiotherapy, and yes, those treatments come with side effects — but so does life! The bottom line is, these methods are backed by extensive scientific research and have been proven to be effective in treating cancer. Natural medicine certainly has its place and can complement traditional treatments through holistic care, but to suggest that it can replace established therapies is not only naive but potentially dangerous. Ignoring proven medical interventions in favor of anecdotal "cures" could mean playing a risky game with your health. So, if you're facing a cancer diagnosis, I strongly suggest having a serious conversation with your oncologist instead of getting swayed by a charismatic pitch for "natural" solutions. Your life literally depends on it!
Answer_with_user_profile: It's understandable to seek alternatives when confronted with a cancer diagnosis, especially when treatments like chemotherapy and radiotherapy are labeled as toxic. However, it's crucial to approach this topic with caution. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy are established medical treatments with a solid body of evidence supporting their effectiveness in targeting and killing cancer cells. While these treatments can have side effects, many patients find them necessary for fighting cancer—and the potential benefits often outweigh the risks. In contrast, claims that natural medicine can cure cancer are not universally supported by scientific research. There are various herbal remedies and natural therapies that may assist with symptom management or help bolster the immune system, but none have been conclusively proven to cure cancer on their own. If you choose to explore alternative therapies, it's essential to consult with an oncologist or a medical professional who understands both conventional and natural treatments. They can help you build a comprehensive plan that includes evidence-based treatments and discusses any alternative options safely. Always be wary of individuals promoting "miracle cures" without scientific backing, as this can lead to delayed treatment and poorer outcomes. Your health is paramount, and informed decisions based on solid evidence can make a substantial difference in your cancer journey.
Answer_with_full_information: While the allure of natural medicine can be strong, it's crucial to approach cancer treatment with a well-informed perspective. It's true that chemotherapy and radiotherapy can have significant side effects, as they target rapidly dividing cells, which can include healthy tissues along with cancerous ones. However, these treatments have been extensively researched and are supported by a myriad of clinical studies demonstrating their effectiveness in treating various types of cancer. The term "toxic" can often be misleading; many conventional treatments aim to eradicate cancer cells and improve survival rates. On the other hand, the efficacy of natural medicine remains a contentious issue. While some natural remedies may offer supportive care and improve quality of life, they should not be seen as substitutes for scientifically validated treatments. It's important to understand that cancer is a complex disease, and what works for one person may not work for another. If you're considering alternative therapies, it’s advised to consult with your oncologist or a healthcare professional who understands both conventional and alternative treatments. They can help you navigate the available options, ensuring that any approach you choose will be safe and can be integrated effectively with standard therapies. Remember, cancer treatment is not a one-size-fits-all scenario; it requires a careful balance of evidence-based practices and, if desired, complementary approaches that align with your personal values and preferences. Always prioritize your health and safety in the decision-making process.

Question: If you were a patient, what would you do if you felt your doctor was rushing you through your appointment?
Old_Answer: Just the other day, my girlfriend told me a horrific story about a patient who was basically neglected by his former urologist. The 42-year-old patient had been diagnosed with testicle cancer and was nervously waiting for therapies to begin, but for some obscure reason his urologist did not make the time to come up with the appropriate medical answer, and brushed the patient off as soon as he frantically entered the consultation room yet again. And so the patient decided to ask for a second opinion in another hospital. When my girlfriend gave him a physical last Friday, she indeed found the tumor in his left testicle — it had considerably grown, and the testicle was bound to be removed. But after further inspection, she also felt a lump in the other testicle which had not been detected by the patient’s former urologist. And this testicle has to be removed too. Fortunately the patient already has children, but in any case some nontrivial permanent hormonal treatments are awaiting him to prevent him to become a female essentially, plus the psychological weight of a life without testicles (which might sound funny, but definitely is not). So if you really think you are being rushed through your appointments by your MD — certainly if something serious is lying beneath — you may want to ask for a second opinion. It’s your life after all. SOURCES: Anatomy of the penis (Gray’s illustration).[1]
Answer_with_writing_sample: If I were a patient in that situation, I would channel my inner advocate and not hesitate for a second to raise my concerns. After all, it’s my health on the line, right? I’d start by making eye contact, slowing down my speech a bit, and asking direct questions like, “Can we take a moment to discuss my symptoms more thoroughly?” It’s important to assert myself and make it clear that I’m not just another number in their busy schedule. If the doctor continues to brush me off like a pesky fly, I’d seriously consider seeking a second opinion. My health is not something to be rushed — it’s definitely not a drive-thru experience! Who knows, maybe a different doctor might be more than keen to actually listen to what I have to say. In short, I’d remember that I have a voice, and it deserves to be heard, no matter how rushed the appointment feels.
Answer_with_user_profile: If I felt my doctor was rushing me through my appointment, I would first take a moment to assess the situation. It’s important to differentiate between a genuinely busy day for the doctor and a pattern of behavior that makes me feel unheard. If I sensed that my concerns were being overlooked, I would calmly and politely express my feelings. I might say something like, “I appreciate your time, but I have a few concerns that I really want to discuss more in-depth.” This can signal to the doctor that I need more attention. Additionally, I would prepare for future appointments by writing down my questions or concerns beforehand to ensure nothing gets missed, allowing me to be more concise while still addressing everything that’s important to me. If the pattern continued despite my attempts to communicate, I might consider seeking a second opinion or finding another physician who is more aligned with my needs. It's crucial, as a patient, to feel comfortable and to have open lines of communication with healthcare providers. After all, our health and well-being depend on it. Finally, maintaining a constructive attitude, rather than one of confrontation, helps foster a collaborative doctor-patient relationship, which is beneficial for both parties.
Answer_with_full_information: If I felt my doctor was rushing me through an appointment, the first thing I would do is take a deep breath and remind myself that my health is the priority here. It’s easy to feel overwhelmed in a clinical setting, especially in today’s fast-paced world. I’d start by gently asserting my needs. I might say something like, “I really want to ensure I’m addressing all my concerns today; could we take a bit more time?” This not only signals to the doctor that I value thoroughness but also encourages a dialogue rather than a monologue. If that approach doesn’t seem effective, I’d consider asking direct questions that require specific answers to guide the conversation and ensure all my points are covered. For instance, asking about the next steps in my treatment or clarification on medical terminology can help to steer the discussion in a productive direction. If I still felt rushed, I wouldn’t hesitate to express my concerns more explicitly. Phrasing it as “I’m feeling a little rushed, and it’s important to me that we discuss X in greater detail” can encourage the doctor to slow down. Ultimately, if I consistently felt my concerns were sidelined during multiple visits, I’d consider seeking a second opinion or even switching doctors. My health is paramount, and finding a healthcare provider who values genuine communication and partnership is essential. Remember, as a patient, you have the right to be heard, and it's important to advocate for your own health needs.

Old_Answer: In my research institute I have barely seen it, although there is one professor who (in)famously sleeps with his PhD students. (In fact, he married one of them after divorcing his first wife, but the cheating never stopped.) In my girlfriend’s hospital though (and the other hospitals she worked in), the vastness of cheating from both wives and husbands is nothing less than breathtaking. One doctor — dr. Peterson, an orthopedist and serial cheater with a wife and kids at home — at some point simultaneously had a relationship with two nurses who found out about each other, and engaged in a cat fight at a party which I happened to attend. Nowadays, Peterson has a relationship with an anesthesiologist called dr. Paris (who also is married with children), and the running joke among the nurses is that “it turns out he was in Paris again on the weekend.” This is just one of many examples, but usually the relationships develop between female nurses and male doctors — in the mind of many (but not all) nurses, being married to a hospital doctor and bear his children lifts them to the highest echelons, and endows them with the status they always dreamed of. But being in Paris on a regular basis is also rather nice, of course. SOURCES: the drawing is my own.
Answer_with_writing_sample: The answer to this question isn’t as straightforward as a simple yes or no — life in the workplace is often laden with complexities, and the dynamics can be quite surprising. Many people will tout statistics or anecdotes about how often wives cheat while at work, but the reality is often more nuanced. Sure, there are those who may develop connections with colleagues that blur ethical lines, especially in high-stress environments where emotional bonds can form unexpectedly. But, let’s not forget the intricacies of marriage itself; it’s not always about a lack of love or commitment but often stems from deeper issues, such as communication gaps or unmet emotional needs. And while some might indulge in the thrill of a secret affair, many couples navigate these challenges together, working through their concerns rather than stepping outside the boundaries. So, while infidelity can and does happen, attributing it solely to the workplace is like saying all doctors are driven by money — it simplifies a lot of layers that really deserve a closer look. Ultimately, relationships are complex, and each story is unique, making blanket statements not only misleading but also reductive.
Answer_with_user_profile: The question of whether many wives cheat while at work involves complex social dynamics and individual circumstances. While statistics on infidelity can vary, studies suggest that a significant portion of affairs does occur in the workplace. The environment itself often facilitates emotional connections, as colleagues spend extended hours together, sharing experiences and challenges. This proximity can sometimes lead to feelings of intimacy that are difficult to navigate, especially if there are underlying issues in a marriage. It's also important to consider the role of opportunity—being in a workplace where individuals feel comfortable and are frequently interacting can increase the chances of cheating. However, not every wife will succumb to these temptations; many factors play a role, including personal values, the health of the marriage, and individual character. Ultimately, while workplace infidelity does happen, it’s a reflection of a myriad of influences, not just the workplace itself. Maintaining open communication, addressing marital issues, and fostering a healthy emotional connection are crucial in mitigating such risks. Therefore, it's crucial to approach the subject with an understanding of the complex motivations and context behind infidelity rather than generalizing about a specific group of individuals.
Answer_with_full_information: The question of whether many wives cheat while at work is complex and inherently tied to various factors, including individual circumstances, relationship dynamics, and workplace environment. While statistics suggest that cheating can occur in approximately 20-25% of committed relationships, it’s critical to recognize that infidelity is not confined to one gender or circumstance. In cases where individuals feel neglected or unappreciated in their marriages, the workplace may provide a tempting emotional or physical refuge. Moreover, the modern work environment often blurs the boundaries between professional and personal life, which can lead to more opportunities for flirtation and, in some cases, infidelity. It's not uncommon for strong emotional connections to form between coworkers, especially when they share common goals, frustrations, and victories throughout their day. However, this doesn’t mean that cheating is a regular occurrence for the majority of wives. Many women maintain strong ethical standards and prioritize their commitments despite workplace temptations. Ultimately, the reasons behind why any person strays are many and varied, often linked to personal issues rather than simple opportunity. So while it’s fair to acknowledge that it happens, we must be careful not to generalize or assume that a significant number of wives cheat merely because they're at work. Like all aspects of relationships, fidelity is rooted deeply in individual values, commitment, and communication.

Question: As a doctor, what has a patient done that caused you to burst out in laughter?
Old_Answer: The patient was wheeled into the ER with a broken hip, only 52 years old and looking even much younger. And still, something was going on. The surgeon on call told the nurses that the patient had to stay in bed until the operation, and that no matter what, this patient might prove to be a nuisance. Less than thirty minutes later, the patient asked one of the nurses what he was doing in the hospital, and demanded that he leave ASAP — “There is NOTHING wrong with me !” And so the nurse explained that he had an accident and broken his hip, and that he must stay in his bed at all costs until the operation. The patient did not understand his predicament, and became even angrier because he was obviously held here against his will, and for some reason he had forgotten what had happened earlier this week. But in any case, one thing was sure (because he was not crazy): “He had NOT broken his hip, and he was leaving the hospital ASAP !!” And then he jumped off the bed. At first, some of the MDs laughed the whole issue away when they heard about what had happened, but soon after they understood that the patient really had jumped off the bed. And they all knew what happens to a broken hip when it hits the floor again. But this particular patient suffered from young on-set dementia, and he simply forgot what he was told, and then reacted as if he never heard the question. He never had a broken hip though. (Those crazy people.) SOURCES: the medical scans were taken from The Lancet.

It was a delightful moment that humanized the clinical setting, making me realize that our anxieties can definitely manifest in the wildest of ways. Plus, let’s be honest, who wouldn’t crack a smile thinking about the absurdity of a giant crab as a health threat? In the end, it turned out to be a case of sunburn and a little too much beach lounging, but hey, if I ever do write a book, that moment will definitely make the cut!

Question: People with autism who got diagnosed (really) late, what was a dead giveaway you didn’t notice was autism related until you got diagnosed?
Old_Answer: I know I should not do this, but I am doing it anyhow. There is not a single person (with autism) who can answer this question. Which means that any single person who answers this question as an autistic person, is actually not autistic. Let’s first translate the question into a more physical-medical context: “People who got in a wheelchair really late, can you please walk to me to explain when you noticed you could not walk ?” They can’t. Because they can’t walk. They can’t take a stroll because the legs don’t work. (“There was this car accident, you know.”) And autistic patients can’t either. If they suffer from REAL autistic spectrum disorder — with REAL, I mean that as a paraplegic, you don’t have any feeling in your legs so you can’t walk around with a stick — they cannot answer this question. Because real ASD patients do not understand that they have a disorder. The saddest Quora accounts are those which say (in the heading): I am autistic, and proud of it (2,300 answers). Patients — the REAL ones — with ASD do not understand that diagnosis. Do not write answers about their disorder, because the not-understanding is a part of the diagnosis. If you understand and write about it, you don’t have it — not really. If you are able to walk in one way or the other, you are not paraplegic. So, please-please-please, so-called autistic writers on Quora: I know you need attention, and I know you need a way to be special (for some reason). But this is not the way. It’s hard enough to not feel your legs. SOURCES: drawing by Beksiński.

I remember vividly how I would annoy everyone at family gatherings by insisting on sticking to a strict schedule of events, like airport-like boarding protocols for gift unwrapping on Christmas morning. It seemed innocuous enough then—just my quirky preference to keep things orderly—but post-diagnosis, I realized it was a classic symptom of autism, a way to create predictability in a chaotic world. What baffled me even more was how I’d consistently get called “overly serious” or “too rigid,” but in my mind, I was simply managing my anxiety. The realization hit like a brick wall: what I thought was just a childhood quirk was, in fact, a fundamental aspect of my neurodiversity that didn't align with the "norm." And then, of course, I found myself laughing at all those times I particularly zeroed in on minor details, dissecting them to the point where most people would glaze over—what I thought made me detail-oriented turned out to be another giveaway. It's funny how the things that seem most peculiar about us can, in retrospect, become clear markers of something bigger. SOURCES: Personal reflections and anecdotes.

Answer_with_full_information: As someone who's navigated the complexities of late autism diagnosis, I can relate to the feeling of suddenly connecting the dots of past experiences. One glaring “dead giveaway” that stood out in hindsight was my profound struggle with social nuances. Question: Why do contractions hurt during labor?
Old_Answer: A colic occurs when there is an obstruction within a hollow internal organ, such as the intestines, gallbladder, rectum, kidneys, ureters, and uterus. To try to get rid of the obstruction, the smooth muscles inside the walls of the hollow organ contract vigorously around it, and these spasms cause pain. These smooth muscles are involuntary (we cannot control their function) and are controlled by the unconscious part of our brain function using the autonomic nervous system.[1] (In some way it’s our instinct that govern the colic.) And this is where our story gets really interesting. Most people attribute the intense pain associated to labor mainly to the stretching sensations of cervix and uterus, but that is definitely not so: sensory denervation of the uterus occurs during pregnancy and cervical sensory denervation occurs at the onset of labor, so that actually there are no such stretching sensations whatsoever during childbirth — the stretch receptors are totally gone.[2] But where does the actual labor pain come from ? Labor pain occurs due to vasoconstriction within the uterus. When the uterus contracts, there is a reduction in blood flow to the uterus causing hypoxia:[3] This decrease in blood volume causes pain because although the uterus is denervated, the surrounding blood vessels remain innervated, and the disruption of homeostasis causes an imbalance in the system, which results in sensations of pain. So the original “uterine colic” is the bad guy — he (eventually) causes the pain. On a related matter, renal colics are generically considered to be (much) more painful than “uterine colics,”[4] and to add insult to injury, the psychological strength of the pregnant patient determines a big part of the personal perception of childbirth pain. (The lower the pain threshold, the worse the perception.) That’s one reason why the breathing method really works. And although natural childbirth is usually very painful, it is not the worst pain in the world, nor the most painful medical condition in the world — of course. Otherwise, who would go for a second baby without an epidural ? SOURCES: the footnoted sites. For the image: Emile Beau: Grossesse gémellaire. To put it plainly, contractions are the uterus's way of doing some serious heavy lifting — literally. As the muscles tighten and relax, they are working hard to push that adorable little human out into the world, and in the process, those powerful muscles can create a whole lot of pressure and discomfort. And let’s not forget the emotional aspect; the anticipation and anxiety that come with labor can amplify the discomfort manifold. So there you have it: contractions are basically your body’s muscular symphony, playing out a painful, yet somehow beautiful, crescendo as it readies itself for an equally dramatic finale. Question: What are some sad truths about life?
Old_Answer: Nicole is the 74-old-mother of one of my best friends, and on Saturday she had a long talk with us because she needed someone to talk to. It was at the birthday party of her grandson — who also is my godson (terrible term) — and her oldest sister was there as well. Aunt Lynn, a proud educated woman of 87 whom Nicole considers to be her mom, rather than her sister. Aunt Lynn has been a single and extremely independent woman for most of her life, and I have known her at a personal level for at least fifteen years. But something has changed. She still drives a car, but since about a year, she often gets lost when she tries to visit her little sister (only a couple of blocks down the road), and has to drive back. She always dressed meticulously in the past, following old etiquette rules, but nowadays she often walks around in her pajamas, not really realizing what she is doing. Or what day it is. She also virtually stopped bathing. My friend’s family is conservative, and the word “dementia” has never been mentioned in conversations — she “forgets a lot” and “has a hard time remembering what she was talking about” — but not the word (as if saying the word will only make matters worse). The last time I saw Aunt Lynn (before Saturday), it was unclear to me how bad her memory was affected by her condition, and also on Saturday, I thought she was doing really well for a 87-year-old. Until she ordered drinks. All of a sudden, she grabbed my friend — her nephew — by the arms, and ordered drinks for some people. And on the verge of being aggressive, she urged him to hurry up, because she was tired of waiting. We thought she was kidding at first. Only, she wasn’t. Her sister Nicole was extremely worried (because the mental deterioration of Aunt Lynn has progressed really rapidly in the past months), and she tried to convince her sister to call it a day, and head back home with her. But Aunt Lynn refused altogether, and stated “that this was HER house, and that SHE would decide what happened IN HER HOUSE.” Only it wasn’t her house at all — it was my friend’s. She never lived there (not even close). In the end, Aunt Lynn was so confused that she joined her little sister to go back home, speechless and confused, as if she was a toddler who needed a nap. And I saw the tears in Nicole’s eyes, and realized that an era was nearing its very gloomy end. And that nothing will be left of Aunt Lynn’s mind apart from scraps and pieces, wrapped up in aggressive episodes of frustration, while every next tick of the clock will obliterate her even further, and every next question will confuse her even more. And that is the saddest thing about Aunt Lynn. That if she will even take a few more steps down the ladder of oblivion, suddenly all letters and sounds will be lost, and only the bleakest emptiness will remain — And with any luck, one last smile. SOURCES: painting by Mikhail Vasilyevich Nesterov.
